Title: Cash transfers and social preferences of children
Authors: Johannes Haushofer, Magdalena Larreboure, Sara Lowes, Leon Mait

Title: Fostering institutional trust and organ donation: Evidence from a randomized informational intervention in Tunisia
Abstract: Organ transplantation saves lives and improves the quality of life of patients who would otherwise depend on costly and invasive treatments. The technology is becoming available in low- and middle-income countries, but the gap between the demand for and the supply of organ transplants remains large. In a randomized controlled trial at a Tunisian university, we evaluate an expert-led intervention designed to inform about organ donation and strengthen trust in medical institutions. The intervention consists of a short video testimonial from a heart transplant survivor, a presentation led by a medical doctor and a short Q&A session. We find that the intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive evidence of positive spillover effects on the control group. The survey data provides little support for changes in attitudes and social expectations as potential mechanisms. Instead, it reveals large and statistically significant increases in medical and legal knowledge, religious beliefs supportive of donation, and institutional trust among treated students. Finally, we show that treatment effects on organ donor registration are driven by male students and those whose families likely support organ donation. Targeting older segments of the population may further increase the impact and cost-effectiveness of this intervention.

Title: Perceived need and measured well-being: How well do subjective rankings capture relative poverty?
Authors: Immacolata Ranucci, Kibrom A. Abay, Luca Tiberti
Abstract: Subjective well-being rankings are increasingly used to target social protection programs, yet their ability to capture relative welfare and wealth remains debated. This study benchmarks self-, peer-, and elite-based poverty rankings against consumption- and wealth-based measures using Ethiopian household survey data, where about 20 households per village were ranked from neediest to least needy by themselves, peers, and community leaders. We assess concordance between subjective and conventional welfare rankings and explore sources of divergence. Subjective rankings align more with relative wealth than consumption and with total rather than per capita welfare, suggesting they overlook household composition. Elite-based rankings best capture conventional measures, followed by peers’ and self-rankings. Subjective rankings also better reflect relative deprivation among households exposed to covariate shocks. A composite index combining all three improves agreement with standard metrics. Information asymmetries, favoritism, and welfare dynamics partly explain discrepancies, offering insights for enhancing targeting in data-scarce settings.

Title: The economics of abduction marriage: Evidence from Ethiopia
FDI spillovers in history: Interwar Japanese “Zaikabo” investment in China's cotton spinning industry
Authors: Holger Görg, Toshihiro Okubo, Eric Strobl, Maximilian Von Ehrlich
Abstract: We estimate productivity spillovers from Japanese cotton-spinning firms in China (known as Zaikabo) to local Chinese cotton-spinning mills based on plant-level data for 1925 to 1938. In order to capture the important role of distance in facilitating such spillovers we geo-localised the plants. Our results provide clear evidence for positive spillovers from Zaikabo to local Chinese mills, which go hand-in-hand with an upgrade in production technology towards greater use of capital. Spillovers are very localised, being strongest within a radius of up to 10 km around the Zaikabo and particularly strong for mills in Shanghai. Exploiting information on the workforce composition of the Japanese affiliates, we find suggestive evidence of a skilled-labour channel: spillovers tend to be larger from Zaikabo employing higher shares of skilled labour. We also find some evidence in line with the idea that these gains are larger for Chinese mills with higher initial productivity, consistent with a role for absorptive capacity. Our paper is the first to document FDI productivity spillovers in a historical context and to characterise the channels through which they operate.

Title: Corruption and capital investment: Worldwide evidence
Under pressure: High-Stakes exams and media-reported student suicides in India
Abstract: We estimate the temporal association between high-stakes exam timing and media-reported student suicides in India using geocoded news data. Student suicides are 17.5 percent higher during months in which NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examinations are held, with no comparable pattern around lower-stakes board exams or among adults. The association is concentrated when national entrance exams coincide with board exams, suggesting the salience of cumulative exam burden. These patterns are stronger among girls, in states with higher exam participation, and in urbanised districts. Event-study estimates show suicides increasing immediately before and during exams, while movements around result announcements are weaker and less precisely estimated. We find no evidence that broad shifts in media attention during cyclone or election months account for the pattern, although exam-specific reporting bias cannot be ruled out. In the absence of mental health data, we generate an alternative database to address a policy question and spur future research.

Title: Payroll taxes, firm dynamism, and aggregate productivity
Authors: Jin Feng, Yuting Li, Yu Liu
Abstract: This study examines the impact of payroll-tax enforcement on firm dynamism and its implications for aggregate productivity. We exploit China's Social Security Collection Agency Reform, which transferred responsibility for collecting social-insurance contributions from local social-insurance agencies to tax authorities, thereby strengthening enforcement. We show that the reform increased firms’ social-insurance contributions, shifted workers toward informal employment without reducing overall nonagricultural employment, and reduced new firm entry while weakening incumbent firms’ profitability and investment. Overall, the reform reduced measured aggregate productivity in China's registered, above-scale industrial sector by 3.3 percent, with entry into the above-scale industrial sector accounting for about 45 percent of the estimated decline.

Title: Familiar faces, honest answers? The impacts of enumerator familiarity and modality on survey responses
Authors: Travis Baseler, Lipeng Chen, Thomas Ginn

Title: Editorial Board
The economic gains from breaking boundaries: Reformulating index insurance zones to maximize lower tail dependence
Authors: Enrique Estefania-Salazar, Michael R. Carter, Eva Iglesias, Álvaro Escribano
Abstract: Index insurance intended to help low-wealth households manage risk is hampered by downside basis risk, meaning that the insured suffers a loss, but the insurance index fails to signal a loss. Existing index insurance contracts use statistically ad hoc administrative boundaries to demarcate insurance zones. We develop an algorithm that creates zones that maximize lower tail dependence amongst individual units included in each zone. Breaking boundaries in this way minimizes basis risk. Using data from a satellite-based index insurance program in Kenya, we show that replacing administrative with optimized zones can as much as triple the value of insurance using an expected utility-based metric of insurance quality.

Title: Picking winners: Local land allocation and bottom-up industrial policy in China
Authors: Wenjia Tian, Zhi Wang, Qinghua Zhang
Abstract: This study examines the industrial preferences of local governments in China through the lens of land allocation. We analyze industrial land transactions from 2007 to 2019, a period marked by both expanding industrial policy and intensifying land market competition. Using a border discontinuity design that compares land transactions near county borders, we separate local government preferences from firm demand. We find systematic industrial favoritism: localities offer deeper price discounts to industries aligned with their existing specialization. This favoritism persists over time, is more pronounced in industries with substantial unrealized agglomeration potential, and is stronger in regions with well-developed market institutions. We further show that local governments comply with upper-level industrial policy only when it aligns with their own specialization. Together, these findings point to a bottom-up process in which local governments use land allocation to attract firms that reinforce local industrial strengths through agglomeration spillovers.

Title: Supporting learning in and out of school: Experimental evidence from India
Abstract: Although targeted educational interventions for primary school children in low-income countries have led to substantial improvements in learning, the extent of their effectiveness varies considerably across studies, raising questions about how to adapt them to different settings. This paper examines a novel primary education program that combines a conventional in-school targeted pedagogical intervention with an out-of-school study group initiative facilitated by the community. We use a cross-cutting randomized experiment design across 200 villages in Assam, India. Our results show that standalone implementation of either component has no significant effect on learning outcomes, but when the components are combined in the full program they improve children’s test scores in mathematics and language by 0.11 and 0.09 standard deviations, respectively. The analysis highlights that the combined program increases program awareness and take-up, thereby increasing program effectiveness.

Title: Is drug-related violence fueling emigration from Central America?
Authors: Leonardo Bonilla-Mejía, Jessica Bracco, Andrés Ham, Leonardo Peñaloza-Pacheco
Abstract: We examine how drug-related violence influences emigration choices in Central America, a region that has experienced a sharp increase in migration to the United States. Combining multiple data sources, we leverage an instrumental variables strategy that exploits local variation in proximity to drug-trafficking routes and coca production in Colombia. Our results show that rising violence increases intentions, plans, and preparations to emigrate, particularly to the United States. These migration responses are strongest among young and higher-skilled individuals. Mediation analysis suggests that these migration responses operate predominantly through declining economic activity and worsening labor-market conditions in Central America, rather than through a direct response to insecurity.

Title: Race-to-the-bottom dynamics in industrial land pricing: Asymmetric effects of China’s 2009 price floor adjustment policy
Authors: Ran Tao, Jialin Yu, Zhejin Zhao
Abstract: Minimum price floors are a common but understudied instrument for regulating industrial land markets in developing economies. We exploit China's 2009 adjustment of minimum industrial land prices, which lowered the minimum land price in some counties and raised it in others. Combining parcel-level land transactions with county characteristics in a difference-in-differences design, we find a striking asymmetry: easing counties experienced a 9.15% decline in industrial land prices and a 23.12% expansion in transferred area, whereas tightening counties showed no detectable change. The asymmetry reflects the floor's initial binding status: it was binding in easing counties, where competition for mobile manufacturing capital pushed prices down and expanded land supply, but non-binding in tightening counties, where the raised floor either stayed below market prices or was offset through rebates and subsidies. Easing counties also gained 15.53% more large-scale industrial enterprises relative to the sample mean and 7.90% in fiscal revenue, yet new land sales concentrated in low- and medium-low-tech, land-intensive sectors, a pattern that persisted through 2022 with no shift toward higher-tech industries. Relaxing a binding industrial land price floor thus brings short-run gains in firm entry and fiscal revenue but leaves these counties specialized in low-tech industries, consistent with race-to-the-bottom competition operating through industrial land pricing.

Title: Turning Inward and/or Outward: Which socioemotional skills pay for agribusiness entrepreneurs in Nigeria?
Authors: Smita Das, Clara Delavallade, Ayodele Fashogbon, Sreelakshmi Papineni
Abstract: Socioemotional skills programs are widely used to promote economic empowerment, yet their returns may depend on the type of skills targeted and social context. We study this question using a randomized controlled trial (RCT) among 4,500 aspiring agribusiness entrepreneurs in Nigeria within a large-scale government program. Participants were randomly assigned to an interpersonal-skills curriculum, a combined interpersonal and intrapersonal-skills curriculum of the same length, or a control group. Both trainings substantially increase women's business performance, raising average profits by 50%. The two trainings generated broadly similar economic impacts overall. Effects are largest in communities with more liberal gender norms, where women report improvements in interpersonal skills such as empathy and negotiation, and better relational outcomes. Despite large economic gains, we find no corresponding increases in women's empowerment or intrahousehold decision-making. For men, interpersonal-skills training increases household income, while the combined curriculum raises profits but only in the most gender-liberal environments. The results show that the returns to socioemotional skills programs depend not only on which skills are taught, but also on whether prevailing social norms permit individuals to express and deploy those skills. Translating gains into broader empowerment may require complementary programs that relax gender norms.

Title: Road to resilience: Floods, highways and Indian informal manufacturing
Abstract: Road infrastructure is widely recognized as a driver of economic development, but can it also aid in disaster resilience? This study addresses the resilience question in the Indian context by examining the output effects of dual and staggered treatments: national highway construction – the Golden Quadrilateral, and the North-South and East-West highways – and extreme flood exposure. Employing a production-theoretic framework, this study focuses on India’s informal manufacturing, the largest in the world without any formal safety nets. It combines geospatially matched, staggered flood exposure data from the Dartmouth Flood Observatory with phased highway rollout timelines from the National Highways Authority of India and repeated cross-section plant-level survey data (1990–2016). Exploiting quasi-random variation in the timing of flood exposure and road construction, a stacked difference-in-differences design is implemented, matching treated districts to future-treated counterparts. Results show that floods significantly reduce gross output and value added, while access to completed highway segments nearly offsets the average 8 percent flood-related output loss through higher output and reduced input expenditures. These effects are magnified for plants that own transport assets, highlighting a complementarity between internal logistics and external infrastructure. Off-highway plants exhibit similar resilience only when they possess transport assets. Heterogeneity analysis by market orientation reveals that resilience benefits are higher among non-tradable industries through local market stabilization. These findings reveal that roads are not only engines of development but also critical to disaster resilience. Designing infrastructure with dual function— development and resilience —is essential for building a climate-smart and resilient economy.

Title: The power of words: Adult literacy campaign and intergenerational transmission of human capital
Authors: Shuo Chen, Zhuoer Lin, Xian Xu, Yanfei Yin
Abstract: We examine the intergenerational impact of China's 1950s adult literacy campaign, one of the largest anti-illiteracy efforts in history, reaching 150 million people. While direct effects on adult literacy remain debated, we document significant long-term benefits for the next generation's education. Using an original dataset compiled from county gazetteers and the population census, we find a notable increase in educational attainment for children whose parents were more strongly exposed to the campaign. We attribute these results to extensive government propaganda that likely shifted population attitudes toward education. Our findings suggest that education campaigns can be a viable strategy in developing countries for improving human capital.

Title: The long shadow of typhoons: Prenatal exposure and adult mental health
Authors: Yu-Ting Huang, Elaine M. Liu, Jin-Tan Liu, Tzu-Yin Hazel Tseng
Abstract: This paper examines how poor in utero conditions caused by severe typhoons affect psychological well-being later in life. We exploit variation in the timing and location of severe typhoon landfalls. Our design compares individuals with higher expected fetal exposure in landfall counties to those with no such exposure. A one-unit increase in expected in utero exposure raises the likelihood of an adult mental illness diagnosis by 2.2 percentage points, or 11 percent relative to the mean. The incidence of mood disorders such as depression and the use of antidepressants has risen by more than 50 percent. The adverse effects are concentrated among women. In a fully interacted model, we reject equality of the male and female effects for our main outcomes. This gender gap is not driven by differential healthcare-seeking behavior. We discuss several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms that could generate a genuinely female-concentrated effect, including sex-specific fetal programming and mortality selection.

Title: Refugee immigration and natives’ fertility
Authors: Aya Aboulhosn, Cevat Giray Aksoy, Berkay Ozcan
Abstract: Research and policy debates on population ageing typically assume that immigration matters only through immigrants’ own fertility and its impact on total population size, ignoring effects on natives’ fertility. We study this margin in the context of the large inflow of Syrian refugees into Türkiye after 2011. Using an instrumental-variables strategy, we provide evidence that greater local exposure to refugees increases native fertility. Drawing on complete birth histories from the Demographic and Health Surveys, we find that the response operates primarily through earlier entry into motherhood and is concentrated among younger women. The result holds across three independent datasets, including administrative birth registers, and is mirrored in women's stated ideal number of children. Examining potential mechanisms, we find the evidence most consistent with improved household economic security and find no support for channels operating through housing costs or the use of paid childcare.

Title: The political economy of regional development: Evidence from the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno
Abstract: Devolution of authority over public investments can lead to agency problems and trigger tactical redistribution between different tiers of government. We test this hypothesis in the context of the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno: a massive development programme for Southern Italy (1950-1984). By 1971, the authority over funds allocation was transferred from a centralised committee to the newborn regional governments. We combine unique historical data on local administrators with detailed information on projects, and find that, after devolution, municipalities aligned with the regional government were assigned a higher number of projects, without producing any positive impact on long-run economic outcomes.

Title: Self-medication under uncertainty: Insights on drug quality and consumer behavior in Burkina Faso
Authors: Renate Hartwig, Moumouni Koala, Lena Merkel, Salfo Ouedraogo, Fadima Yaya Bocoum
Abstract: How does drug quality affect self-medication behavior? We address this question in the context of Burkina Faso, where self-medication with antibiotics is widespread. Using chemical quality tests, we find that one in three antibiotics on the market is substandard or falsified, posing significant health risks. While consumers are broadly aware of the prevalence of poor-quality drugs, they struggle to assess quality based on observable cues such as price or packaging. To identify causal effects, we conduct a novel lab-in-the-field experiment that varies the probability of purchasing effective medicine. We find that self-medication increases as drug quality becomes more certain. These results suggest that market-level interventions to improve drug quality may unintentionally increase inappropriate antibiotic use, with implications for health policy and antimicrobial resistance.

Title: Reciprocity and state capacity: Evidence from a national pollution control reform in China
Authors: Yu Luo, Yongwei Nian, Ming-ang Zhang
Abstract: We propose a new approach to pollution control from the social contract perspective, which highlights the reciprocal obligations between firms and the government, in contrast to the conventional regulatory view. Combining granular data on Chinese industrial firms with a 2007 reform that sharply increased the government's incentives for pollution control, we show, in a difference-in-differences framework, that firms with prior government support achieved greater emission reductions than those without following the reform, primarily through costly clean technology adoption and output cuts. These effects are consistent across various strategies that account for the potential endogeneity of government support and appear to be driven by reciprocity between firms and the government, as (a) the effects are more pronounced in regions with stronger norms of reciprocity, and (b) the government, in turn, responded with continued support. Alternative explanations—including government leverage, financial constraints, regulatory enforcement, and political connections—cannot explain our findings. We further examine the aggregate implications of firm-government reciprocity at the city level, exploiting quasi-random variation in city-level support induced by plausibly exogenous mayoral rotation and across-mayor variation in support preferences in an instrumental variable design. We find that such reciprocity translated into significant declines in regional pollution concentrations, thereby enhancing the government's capacity for pollution control.

Title: Household consumption and savings over the life cycle: The roles of demographics and durables
Authors: Neha Bairoliya, Areendam Chanda, Jingyi Fang, Fang Yang
Abstract: The canonical prediction of life-cycle models, that individuals smooth consumption over their lifetime, has mostly been tested in developed countries and found little empirical support. We provide a novel developing-country perspective by analyzing patterns of life-cycle consumption, income, and savings rates in India. In contrast to the U.S., Indian households exhibit little growth in nondurable consumption expenditures after adjusting for family size. Surprisingly, this flat adjusted profile coexists with substantial income growth and a sharp rise in the savings/surplus rate over the life cycle. We show that lumpy non-housing durable accumulation is an important use of this life-cycle surplus, helping reconcile high savings rates with flat measured adult-equivalent nondurable consumption. Quantitatively, non-housing durable stock growth accounts for about one-third of accumulated life-cycle surplus by age 45, and an augmented expenditure profile that adds imputed non-housing durable investment flows to nondurables raises adult-equivalent life-cycle growth from 8.4% to 27.9%.

Title: Dual-track in the family: How spousal state employment fuels entrepreneurship
Authors: Wenchao Li, Yifan Lin, Junjian Yi, Haochen Zhang
Abstract: China's rapid growth alongside extensive state ownership challenges theories of state-sector inefficiency. This paper identifies a novel micro-level channel: “dual-track in the family,” whereby one spouse's stable state job enables the other to pursue private entrepreneurship. Using a triple-difference design that exploits the 1993 market reform, we find that spouses of state employees were 9.8 percentage points more likely to become entrepreneurs after the reform. Mechanism evidence suggests that spousal state employment may promote entrepreneurship by insuring the family against risk. The findings reveal how a gradualist, dual-track transition can succeed partly by leveraging state-sector stability to underpin private-sector dynamism.

Title: Migration incentives and elderly health: Evidence from the Hukou reforms in China
Authors: Wei Huang, Hai Huang, Haotian Zhang, Wei Zheng
Abstract: This paper studies the impact of child migration on outcomes of elders who stay behind: consumption, economic participation, health, and mental health. Exploiting variation from the preexisting ties between provinces interacted with the time-varying intensity of regional migration deregulation, we find that increased incentives for internal migration in China resulted in more remittances to rural households, boosting consumption and reducing farm work among the elderly who stay behind. The paper also shows improved healthcare utilization and physical health in these non-migrating elderly populations. However, child migration came with a potential downside: the modest decline in the mental well-being of elderly individuals, possibly due to a lack of informal care and companionship from migrated children. These findings show how internal migration impacts the health and economic wellbeing of elderly individuals in developing countries. (JEL I15, J18, O18, P25, P36, R23)

Title: Career guidance and investments in education: Experimental evidence from Cambodia
Authors: Esther Gehrke, Friederike Lenel, Claudia Schupp
Abstract: Students in low-income contexts often lack guidance in their career decisions, which can lead to a misallocation of educational investments. We report on a randomized field experiment conducted with 1715 students in rural Cambodia and show that a half-day career guidance workshop designed to support adolescents in developing occupational aspirations on average increased educational investments. We document substantial heterogeneity in treatment effects by baseline student performance. While the workshop increased schooling efforts of high-performing students, treated low-performing students reduced their educational investments. We develop a simple model that explains this treatment effect heterogeneity by baseline performance.

Title: The effect of disaster relief on climate adaptation: Evidence from floods in Pakistan
Abstract: Extreme weather events are expected to increase with climate change. Government relief programs are designed to ameliorate the negative consequences, but moral hazard models suggest they also reduce adaptation, such as migrating from disaster-prone areas. Using difference-in-differences, we study the long-term effects of cash relief on migration after the 2010 Pakistan floods. Combining survey and population data, we show that cash transfers have two countervailing effects. As expected, they reduce migration through a moral hazard effect and by facilitating in-situ adaptation. However, they also increase migration by providing liquidity. In practice, these effects cancel each other out in flooded areas.

Title: Building infrastructure and cohesion through locally embedded institutions: Evidence from a field experiment in War-torn Eastern Congo
Authors: Eric Mvukiyehe, Julie Bousquet, Marijke Verpoorten
Abstract: A defining feature of many Community-Driven Development (CDD) interventions in wartorn countries is their pursuit of transformative objectives, seeking to (re)shape local decisionmaking institutions in the process. In recent years, there has been a push to overhaul CDD approaches, with a focus on more realistic objectives aimed at providing infrastructure and building capacity of existing local institutions. We investigate, through a large-scale field experiment involving 400 communities in eastern Congo, the effects of a CDD program that embodied this new focus. Our strategy allows us to identify causal impacts of the CDD intervention, in its basic form consisting of a US$100,000 envelope to finance an infrastructure project with an emphasis on ‘local content’, as well as when augmented with a complementary conflict mitigation component. While the intervention successfully delivered visible infrastructure projects, we find no detectable effects on social cohesion, (violent) conflict, or economic welfare. We conclude discussing policy implications.

Title: Expected foreign military intervention and demand for state-building: Evidence from Mali
Authors: Alessandro Belmonte, Désirée Teobaldelli, Davide Ticchi
Abstract: We study the informational effects of foreign military intervention on citizens’ motivations to participate in state-building processes. We analyze the 2012 United Nations Security Council resolution that authorized intervention in Mali to reunify the country and restore democracy during a profound institutional crisis. By exploiting the randomness of the foreign intervention announcement, relative to the timeline of the Afrobarometer interviews, we document that individuals interviewed the days after the announcement have a higher intrinsic motivation to comply with taxes, are less inclined to refuse to filing taxes, and are more reluctant to evade even if had chances, relative to individuals, interviewed immediately before, with the same characteristics, region, and ethnic group. We demonstrate that these effects are specific to regions characterized by low state capacity and limited ethnic diversity, as well as to individuals who perceive that their ethnic group has not been systematically discriminated against by the state. Consistently with our story, we document that motivations to comply only increase in respondents with access to the news at home (who own either a TV or a radio). Our results survive a wide range of falsification tests and indicate that foreign military interventions signal state-building, raising the expected benefits to participate.

Title: When wages rise, quality falls: Minimum wages and the hidden trade-off in competitive e-commerce markets
Authors: Xinyu Liu, Han Xiao, Songqing Jin
Abstract: We show that product and service quality serve as a hidden margin of adjustment to minimum wage hikes in hyper-competitive digital markets. Leveraging granular transaction data from 2628 Tmall stores in rural China from 2015 to 2020, combined with household surveys and firm-level data, we exploit staggered city-level minimum wage increases and find that in the short run, firms neither reduce employment nor significantly raise prices. Instead, they systematically degrade quality, as evidenced by worse product ratings, slower logistics, and poorer customer service, starting within two quarters and persisting over time. The reduction in intermediate inputs compromises product quality, while cuts to outsourced IT services undermine service quality by weakening operational efficiency. Crucially, this decline is driven by high-quality incumbents, whereas low-quality firms show no change but are more likely to exit the market following the shock. These results reveal a trade-off between labor income and consumer welfare, a cost that is invisible in traditional labor market evaluations but central to a complete welfare assessment.

Title: Exploitation vs. Exploration: How knowledge spillovers shape healthcare practices and innovation
Authors: Yinan Liu, Chen Lin, Zixiao Li, Jing Zhang
Abstract: Improving public service quality is a central challenge in developing countries. A common policy tool is to transfer expertise and protocols to lower-tier institutions, with the expectation that such spillovers improve both current performance and long-term innovative capacity. We study this policy logic using a Chinese reform that mandated knowledge transfer from elite to lower-tier hospitals. Our analysis combines a novel measure of lower-tier hospitals’ alignment with elite hospitals’ clinical practice, developed with a large language model applied to clinical texts and prescription decisions, with measures of physicians’ exploratory activity based on academic publications. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that the policy increased practice alignment at targeted hospitals by 0.29 standard deviations, yielding immediate efficiency gains. At the same time, this gain in exploitation was accompanied by a decline in exploration: physician academic output fell, with publication counts declining by 7% and citation impact by 13%. Our findings highlight that policies promoting existing knowledge can close practice gaps and improve care efficiency, while also creating a potential trade-off with professionals’ incentives to generate new knowledge.

Title: From catastrophe to culture: The role of historical disasters in shaping long-term orientation
Authors: Meng Liu, Jun Wang, James B. Ang, Per G. Fredriksson
Abstract: Natural disasters expose societies to an external environment that requires forward-looking adaptation. This paper argues that societies with greater historical exposure to natural disasters are more likely to develop long-term-oriented norms that emphasize preparation, saving, and future well-being. We test this hypothesis by linking historical exposure to earthquakes, tsunamis, and volcanic eruptions from 4360 BC to 1980 CE to contemporary long-term orientation. Disaster exposure is proxied by a distance-based measure that aggregates proximity to major catastrophic events over long horizons. Long-term orientation is examined using folklore traditions at the ethnic level and survey-based evidence at the individual and country levels. Across all levels of analysis, we find that greater cumulative disaster exposure is associated with significantly stronger long-term orientation. Evidence from folklore and second-generation migrants suggests that these effects operate through cultural adaptation and intergenerational transmission.

Title: Who drives inequality?
Abstract: Which countries drive global inequality? Which states drive US inequality? We characterize the class of inequality measures that can answer these questions, permitting both an additive decomposition by subgroup and a multiplicative decomposition into within- and between-group components. Its central measure is simply the expected ratio of incomes between two randomly selected individuals. We show that global inequality fell since 1990, driven by declining disparities between countries. Inequality is primarily driven by large middle-income countries (India, China) and poor countries (Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia). In the US, rising inequality is explained by widening gaps within states, while between-state inequality remains limited.

Title: Property rights and market frictions: Evidence from the universe of land dispute files in China
Abstract: This research demonstrates how securing land property rights can mitigate frictions in rural land rental markets, specifically in the form of landlord-tenant disputes. By combining a comprehensive data set of land rental dispute records, farm-level panel data, and complete agricultural firm registration data, we find that rental disputes decreased following China's land titling reform. We corroborate this finding by distinguishing between property rights-related disputes (e.g., ownership ambiguity, boundary issues, or expropriation) and contractual enforcement disputes (e.g., rent collection). Further analysis reveals that the effect is particularly pronounced in rental agreements between farmers and agricultural firms, especially those involving non-local entities.

Title: Money and gender: Proxy respondents and the mismeasurement of income in surveys
Authors: Ricardo Estrada, Daniela Goyheix, María Lombardi
Abstract: When sampled individuals are not found at home, many surveys rely on a proxy respondent: another knowledgeable household member. We study the effect of proxy reporting on the measurement of labor income in Mexico. For identification, we use the panel structure of the Mexican labor force survey and compare workers’ reported earnings when they report them themselves to their reported earnings when another household member does the reporting. We find that male workers’ monthly earnings are 7.2% lower when reported by a proxy, whereas female workers’ earnings are only 1.8% lower. We provide evidence that this gender gap reflects both compositional effects, linked to men's higher earnings, and household informational asymmetries, partly driven by men's greater propensity to hide income from other household members. Finally, we study the implications of using proxy respondents and find that it can lead to an underestimation of the gender wage gap by 25%.

Title: Monitoring and delivering: Evidence from dropout rates in Brazil
Abstract: This paper provides evidence that audits can be an effective instrument for improving public services, depending on institutional and sectoral conditions. Leveraging randomized audits of municipal funds in Brazil, I show that audits led to better outcomes for public school students, but were not as effective in improving the provision of other public services. Using a difference-in-differences strategy, I show causal evidence that the audits led to a decrease in dropout rates in municipal elementary and middle schools by 0.41 percentage points (17%), and that this effect persisted for more than eight years. These estimates correspond to approximately one-third of the decrease in dropout rates resulting from the early years of Bolsa Família, a conditional cash transfer program partially designed to minimize student abandonment. The audits were most effective in municipalities where high levels of corruption were uncovered, and whose residents relied heavily on conditional cash transfers.

Title: The youth dividend: Political impacts of demographic transitions
Authors: Rédha Chaba, Michael T. Dorsch, Victor Hiller, Paul Maarek
Abstract: This paper revisits the political economy of transitions to democracy. We extend a canonical rational choice model of democratization by introducing demographic structure, arguing that it shapes the material incentives for political mobilization. Younger cohorts benefit from democratic change over a longer horizon and face lower costs of participation, as they are less economically and socially integrated. As a result, increases in the youth share–such as during the demographic transition–can create a “window of opportunity” for democratization by strengthening the threat of political unrest faced by autocratic elites. We test this prediction using country-year panel data with detailed information on population age structure. Fixed-effects regressions reveal a robust positive relationship between the youth share and the likelihood of democratic improvement. This effect is strongest for the youngest cohorts, in particular individuals aged 15–19. To address concerns about endogeneity, we implement an instrumental variable strategy based on lagged fertility, including variation from neighboring countries. The IV estimates are consistent with the baseline results and are interpreted with appropriate caution. We also show that the effect of the youth share is amplified during economic downturns, highlighting a complementarity between demographic and macroeconomic forces.

Title: The Green Revolution and individualism: Evidence from Indonesia
Authors: Yeonha Jung, Uyseok Lee, Gedeon Lim
Abstract: This paper studies the effects of the Green Revolution, one of the largest development projects in the late 20th-Century, on individualism. We use a difference-in-differences approach to investigate how rapid technological and organizational changes in traditional agriculture reshaped cultural norms in Indonesia, where Green Revolution rollout was largely driven by centralized government interventions. Regions with greater exposure to Green Revolution policies experienced significant and persistent increases in individualism (as measured by a higher prevalence of infrequent names) decades after the end of the program. Results are not driven by pre-trends and hold across a battery of robustness checks. We further document suggestive, correlational evidence of a persistent fall in community funding for public goods, a key measure of collective action. Our findings suggest that technical change can lead to rapid and persistent changes in culture.

Title: Suing the leviathan: The effect of trans-regional jurisdiction reform on corporate investment
Authors: Jiayi Geng, Yinyi Jiao, Jinjun (Ricky) Ke, Meiting Lu, Yaowen Shan
Abstract: We study how the Trans-Regional Jurisdiction reform (TRJ) affects corporate investment. The reform moves administrative lawsuits to courts outside the defendant government's home jurisdiction, which limits local government influence over the courts. We use a stacked difference-in-differences design that draws on the staggered rollout of the reform across cities. We find that the reform raises corporate investment by about 28.7 percent of the sample mean. Complementary evidence shows that the reform improves court outcomes for firms, has stronger effects where pre-reform trust in local institutions is higher, and is associated with lower institutional transaction costs and financing constraints. The effect is larger for firms with more irreversible investment, lower state ownership, and better access to finance. The reform also leads firms to acquire more land and take on more risk, although part of the higher investment appears as overinvestment. These results show how a focused judicial reform can change firm behavior where legal institutions are weak.

Title: Formalized employee search and labor demand
Authors: Lukas Hensel, Tsegay Tekleselassie, Marc Witte
Abstract: Firms in low- and middle-income countries rarely advertise their vacancies formally and instead use social networks to find employees. We experimentally reduce the cost of formal employee search for small and medium-sized enterprises in Ethiopia to test whether informal search constrains the number and type of positions firms create. We find that treated firms increase formal search and shift their labor demand towards more demanding white-collar positions. However, they struggle to fill these newly created vacancies. We provide suggestive evidence that expectations contribute to this result, especially when firms lack prior experience with formal hiring channels: firms appear overly optimistic about the applicant pools formal search will generate, and job-seekers’ wage expectations exceed firms’ wages.

Title: Southern roots abroad: The long-run impact of the Confederate migration to Brazil
Abstract: This paper examines the long-term economic and cultural impacts of the postbellum migration of Southern white individuals to Brazil. Following the U.S. Civil War, thousands of individuals from the former Confederacy settled in a relatively poor region of São Paulo, contributing to its transformation into one of Brazil's wealthiest areas. I show that these migrants, though a small group, played a significant role in regional industrialization, particularly in cotton and textile industries, and in the mechanization of agriculture. Some of the migrants’ cultural traits, such as Protestantism and English language use, persisted over time, largely due to the physical infrastructure they established. Unlike similar migrations within the U.S., I find no evidence of persistent legacies in terms of politics or racial inequality, emphasizing the role of local infrastructure in shaping the economic and cultural outcomes of immigration.

Title: Adult children's human capital accumulation and parents' risky behaviors: Evidence from the higher education expansion in China
Authors: Cong Li, Feng Liu, Linlin Wu, Ruofei Xu
Abstract: This study investigates the upward intergenerational effects of adult children's high-level human capital accumulation on their older parents' risky behaviors. By exploiting the large-scale higher education expansion in China and applying the Treatment Effects Model, we find that children's higher education leads to a significant reduction in their parents' cigarette smoking. However, such effects cannot be found when it comes to an education increase triggered by the compulsory education popularization. These behavior-modifying effects are more pronounced among fathers and less advantaged families, and sons and firstborns within the family play a more effective role in generating such effects. Further evidence is provided for several underlying mechanisms, including increased security in life, more health knowledge, and rural-to-urban migration for older parents. Our findings indicate an about 8.41% contribution to the declining smoking prevalence since the late 1990s, and also imply narrowing health inequality among the older population in the long run.

Title: Editorial Board
Corrigendum to ‘The phantom menace in agriculture: How lagged droughts distort input decisions and create environmental deadweight loss’ [J. Dev. Econ. 182, 2026, 103781]
Authors: Dingqiang Sun, Xueting Qie, Kaixing Huang
Abstract: At the request of the authors, the updated Fig. 6A and B have been included below. The publisher remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims reflected in published maps and institutional affiliations. This change does not affect the scientific content or conclusions of the article.[Figure presented] Fig. 6. Fertilizer overuse caused by responses to past drought.Note: This figure presents the estimated percentage effect (Panel A) and total effect (Panel B) of the responses to past drought on fertilizer use in each province of China (excluding Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan due to lack of data). See the text for details of the calculation and the underlying assumptions.

Title: The match between ‘She’ and ‘Her’: Performance gains from gender match in higher education
Abstract: I use a novel and confidential administrative dataset from a highly rated economics program in Bangladesh to show that female students taught by female instructors gain approximately 9 percent of a standard deviation in grade performance relative to their male counterparts. In addition, I find suggestive evidence that female students benefit more than male students from cumulative exposure to female instructors in longer-term outcomes, such as degree completion time and the likelihood of enrolling in an economics master's program. The quasi-random allocation of students to mandatory courses, where students cannot select either courses or instructors, alleviates self-selection concerns. I rule out the explanation that the gain is driven by gender preference in teachers’ assessment and find that the gain appears to be driven by instructor gender itself rather than by teacher attributes correlated with gender, as the effect remains large and statistically significant even after controlling for observable teacher characteristics.

Title: The effectiveness of entry deregulation: Quasi-experimental evidence from China's export compulsory inspection deregulation
Authors: Zhiqing Yang, Zhiyuan Zhu, Peiyao Liu, Lianfa Luo
Abstract: When and how to phase out existing regulations represents a critical policy issue for developing countries. This paper investigates the effects of export inspection deregulation, exploiting the removal of China's compulsory inspection regulation for export commodities as a quasi-experiment. We construct a unique firm-level panel dataset comprising 8700 observations by mapping 10-digit HS product codes to firm identifiers and integrating four distinct micro-databases. Using a difference-in-differences (DID) framework, we find that deregulating export compulsory inspection exerts an overall positive impact on firm exports, without causing a significant decline in export quality as measured by consumer willingness to pay. We also find that inspection deregulation strengthens firms' innovation capacity, which suggests that innovation could be a mechanism that promotes export performance. Furthermore, we find that the effects of export inspection deregulation are stronger in industries characterized by higher levels of competition. Our findings provide empirical evidence for the benefits of periodic regulatory re-evaluation and suggest that well-designed phase-out mechanisms can foster innovation-led growth in emerging economies.

Title: Securing power, compromising climate: Evidence from drought shocks in China
Authors: Jing Cao, Rong Ma, Yu Zhang
Abstract: This paper examines how natural disasters complicate government efforts to balance energy security with the energy transition in regulated electricity systems. Using random variations in runoff as a natural experiment, we find that droughts lead to a long-term expansion of coal-fired power capacity. This expansion is reflected in extensive-margin adjustments, particularly through the commissioning of new coal-fired power plants. We also show that, under administrative regulation of electricity trading and generation, this investment response is driven primarily by government efforts to strengthen power supply stability rather than by firms’ profit-seeking incentives alone. Our findings highlight how adaptive responses to climate-related supply shocks can generate long-lasting fossil-fuel legacies in developing countries where electricity markets are not yet fully developed.

Title: The spread of (mis)information: A social media experiment in Pakistan
Authors: Sarojini Hirshleifer, Mustafa Naseem, Agha Ali Raza, Arman Rezaee
Abstract: This randomized experiment on a social media platform in Pakistan measures the impact of two treatments that fully control access to misinformation relative to a more standard ex-post approach to controlling misinformation. In the ﬁrst treatment, no misinformation was allowed on the platform, while in the second, it was allowed with an o ﬃ cial rebuttal. The experiment focuses on misinformation regarding COVID-19 and is combined with an intervention to disseminate o ﬃ cial information about the pandemic on the platform. Controlling misinformation through either treatment reduces platform usage. It also reduces exposure to o ﬃ cial information by more than it reduces exposure to misinformation.

Title: Forecasting long-run causal effects
Authors: David Rhys Bernard, Mark Himmelstein, Ezra Karger, Philipp Schoenegger
Abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard in causal inference. However, it is difficult for decision-makers to rely on RCTs when evaluating interventions that affect long-run outcomes. We elicit 25,980 forecasts from 505 participants to test the ability of people to predict the long-run outcomes of RCTs whose results were unknown to participants. Experienced forecasters, academic experts, and laypeople predict the outcomes of seven RCTs, each of which measured long-run outcomes at time horizons of at least five years. Experienced forecasters and academics were more accurate than laypeople, and experienced forecasters outperformed academics, at least in part due to their superior calibration. Aggregated forecasts outperform individual forecasts, showing a clear wisdom-of-the-crowd effect, but neither experienced forecasters nor academics consistently outperform simple benchmarks. We see no evidence of improved forecasting accuracy from randomly providing participants with additional information about good forecasting practices, details about the RCT interventions, or specifics about the local study context.

Title: Labor market competition and inequality
Abstract: We exploit a novel opportunity to study the dynamics of wage inequality and labor market competition over the course of economic development. Our context is Lithuania, where two decades of sustained growth and labor market tightening coincided with a substantial decline in wage inequality. We first fit a two-way fixed-effects model with worker and firm heterogeneity and document that the compression of the variance of firm fixed effects has been the main source of the fall in inequality. Guided by a standard dynamic monopsony model, we then estimate firms’ labor supply elasticities and show that labor market competition has increased over the same period. Finally, we construct a shift-share instrument and provide evidence that new job opportunities created by the accession to the European Union in 2004 contributed to the fall in inequality through their impact on labor market competition in Lithuania.

Title: Who bears the cost: Financial frictions and labor markdown
Authors: Ming Li, Yao Amber Li, Zehao Li
Abstract: We present evidence of a connection between bank concentration and labor markdown in China. Using a large dataset on bank branch distribution and firm performance in China, we document that financial friction in the local market leads to significantly higher firm-level labor markdowns but has little impact on firms’ product markup and profitability. This suggests that firms pass the impact of financial friction to the labor market by exploiting labor when faced with higher financial costs. Such transmission of financial friction is more salient among low-skill-intensity or non-state-owned firms, and greater labor mobility facilitates the transmission. Our findings highlight the distributional effect of financial friction in the economy: labor, especially the low-skilled ones, rather than capital, eventually bears the cost of financial friction.

Title: The forsaken road: Reassessing living standards following the Cuban Revolution and the American embargo
Authors: João Pedro Bastos, Vincent Geloso, Jamie Bologna Pavlik
Abstract: We investigate the causal effects of the 1959 Cuban Revolution on income using a synthetic control approach. We employ a novel dataset with revised GDP estimates that do not rely on the regime's self-reported statistics. We also analyze GDP estimates net of aid coming from the Soviet Union. Our identification strategy allows us to separate the direct effects of the revolution from the diplomatic events that ensued. By overcoming concerns that Cuban GDP statistics are inflated either by the regime's direct manipulation or by Soviet aid, we identify a large decline in Cuban GDP per capita relative to its counterfactual. The decline is larger when accounting for Soviet aid. The embargo only accounts for a minor share of Cuba's under-performance relative to the counterfactual. Our results hold after being subjected to multiple robustness checks and lead to the conclusion that the transition to socialism was the main driver of the inferior economic path Cuba has followed since 1959.

Title: Government demand and firm growth
Authors: Bernard Hoekman, Marco Sanfilippo, Filippo Santi, Rohit Ticku
Abstract: Public procurement in developing countries accounts for approximately 13% of GDP, offering a significant market opportunity for domestic firms, especially those facing demand constraints. This paper explores the impact of selling to government entities on firm performance in Uganda, leveraging detailed administrative data and an event study methodology that corrects for firm self-selection and heterogeneity in the timing of the treatment. The results reveal that while firms increase their total sales after entering government contracts, they do not see improvements in productivity (measured by value added per worker). Moreover, sales to non-government customers drop sharply. This reallocation effect is persistent. This effect is not observed when firms start to sell to large private-sector buyers. Drawing on an original survey of firms engaged in public procurement, we highlight potential drivers of these dynamics, including capacity constraints and profitability differences between public and private sector sales.

Title: Texting parents about early child development: Behavioral changes and unintended social effects
Authors: Oscar Barrera Rodríguez, Karen Macours, Patrick Premand, Renos Vakis
Abstract: Parenting interventions have the potential to improve early childhood development. Text messages are considered a promising channel to diffuse parenting information at low cost. This paper tests whether sending text messages about parenting practices impacts early childhood development. Households in rural Nicaragua were randomly assigned to receive messages about nutrition, health, stimulation and the home environment. The intervention led to significant changes in self-reported parenting practices. However, it did not improve children's cognitive development. When local opinion leaders were randomly exposed to the same text message intervention, parental investments declined and children's outcomes deteriorated. These negative effects were strongest for children of the least educated caregivers. Since interactions between parents and leaders about child development also decreased, the negative effects may have resulted from a crowding-out of efforts by local leaders.

Title: Right-sizing incentives
Authors: Edward N. Okeke, Isa S. Abubakar
Abstract: This paper presents results from a field experiment in Nigeria in which expectant mothers were offered cash payments of N2500, N4000 or N10000 conditioned on using formal medical care. A secondary intervention provided some mothers with an information signal about their pregnancy risk. We find highly non-linear effects of conditional payments-most of the incentive effect occurs on the extensive margin, with rapidly diminishing returns to incentive size. We also uncover new spillover effects: showing that incentives increase healthcare use in childhood by index children and by other children in the household. We find largely null effects of the information signal.

Title: Non-normal Empirical Bayes prediction of local welfare
Authors: Chris Elbers, Roy van der Weide
Abstract: Estimates of the area- and household idiosyncratic error distributions from household income and consumption regression models across 142 household surveys from 16 different countries, the type of models that underpin poverty maps, points to significant deviations from normality. The poverty mapping approach put forward by Elbers et al. (2003) demonstrates the value of accommodating this non-normality. Unfortunately, their non-parametric estimator for the error distribution functions does not lend itself for Empirical Bayes (EB) prediction. This paper puts forward an approach that accommodates both EB prediction and non-normally distributed errors. Accounting for non-normality in Empirical Best estimation of local welfare is found to increase precision relative to normal-EB estimation. While the gains in precision range between substantial and marginal, it is always positive. Being able to obtain precise local estimates of welfare help governments and development agencies identify and monitor lagging areas and allocate their resources in a more efficient manner.

Title: Large-scale land acquisitions in Ethiopia: Impacts on agricultural productivity and deforestation
Authors: Workineh Asmare Kassie, Yeshwas Admasu, Dagim Belay, Solomon Zena Walelign, Jipeng Zhang
Abstract: Large-scale land acquisitions (LSLAs) have expanded rapidly in developing countries and promoted as a pathway to accelerate agricultural transformation. Yet, credible evidence on their developmental and environmental impacts remains limited. This paper provides causal evidence on the effects of LSLAs on agricultural production and forest outcomes by exploiting spatial and temporal variation in the staggered implementation of LSLAs in Gambella, Ethiopia. We combine geo-referenced administrative records on land transactions (2000–2020) with high-resolution remote sensing data on crop production, forest cover, and land use. Using a heterogeneity robust difference-in-difference estimator, we find no evidence that LSLAs increase agricultural production or the share of crop land. In contrast, it leads to significant and persistent declines in tree cover and forest land share. This deforestation-production paradox suggests that, in settings characterized by weak oversight and insufficient infrastructure, poorly regulated large-scale investments can generate substantial environmental burden without delivering the anticipated structural transformation that justifies them.

Title: Housing wealth, family relationship and mental health: Evidence from China
Abstract: Mental health conditions are becoming a significant public health concern in the developing world. This paper examines the impact of housing wealth on an individual's mental health through the lens of family relationships. By leveraging the differential effects of China's National Six Policy, which modified down payment ratios and property deed taxes based on house size, we apply a Regression Discontinuity (RD) design to isolate the causal impact of housing wealth shocks on mental health outcomes. The analysis reveals that individuals experiencing positive housing wealth shocks exhibit lower rates of depression, increased life satisfaction, and greater confidence in the future. Additionally, we find that the effects of housing wealth shocks are particularly pronounced for individuals of lower socioeconomic status. The paper further explores the mechanisms through which housing wealth influences mental health, including improved marital satisfaction, stronger parent-child relationships, increased financial investments in children's education, changes in consumption patterns, alterations in employment status, more leisure time, and reduced health risk behaviors. Our findings underscore the substantial impact of housing wealth on enhancing household well-being, particularly in developing countries.

Title: The benefits of public transit to households: Evidence from India
Abstract: We measure benefits to households from Mumbai's new Metro rail system. We estimate a commute mode choice model to value commute time savings in the short run and a housing choice model to value the improved commuting utility that households experience due to spatial sorting. Aggregate benefits from the Metro rail are over 10 times higher when spatial sorting occurs. In the short run women, college-educated workers, and workers with above median incomes experience higher benefits than their opposites. In the long run, households with lower incomes and assets and less than college education benefit more than their wealthier counterparts.

Title: Local and spillover effects of trade on structural transformation: Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Mateo Hoyos, José Alejandro Coronado, Guilherme Klein Martins
Abstract: This paper investigates the impact of trade liberalization on structural transformation, using quasi-experimental tariff reductions from Brazil's 1990s reforms. Building on recent cross-regional macroeconomic literature, we extend the traditional shift-share framework to estimate both local and spatial spillover effects on sectoral employment shares, providing insights on aggregate outcomes. Regions more exposed to tariff cuts saw declines in manufacturing employment, increases in the primary sector, and reductions in non-tradables. Spillover effects—mediated through migration or proximity—partially offset local deindustrialization in manufacturing but amplified declines in non-tradables. These effects persisted for over twenty years and proved robust to alternative explanations, including competing structural transformation hypotheses and other economic shocks during the period of analysis. Overall, our findings support theories highlighting comparative advantage as a potential driver of trade-induced structural transformation.

Title: From rents to results: China’s anti-corruption reforms and the effectiveness of aid to Africa
Authors: Yiran Du, Kai Feng, Gang Xu
Abstract: The governance practices of donor countries are essential to shaping aid effectiveness. This paper investigates the impact of China's anti-corruption campaign on its aid effectiveness. Leveraging geocoded Chinese aid data and the staggered timing of anti-corruption inspections across aid agencies, we find that the anti-corruption campaign significantly improves the subnational developmental effects of Chinese aid in Africa. Our analysis of the underlying mechanisms suggests that this improvement results not solely from aid being redirected toward better-governed regions, but also from enhanced oversight, efficiency, and information disclosure in project implementation. Finally, we show that China's anti-corruption campaign also alleviates aid-induced spatial inequality in Africa. This study offers novel insights into how domestic donor governance reforms can generate transnational spillover effects that substantially enhance aid effectiveness in recipient countries.

Title: Is high-speed internet detrimental for early childhood development? Evidence from a countrywide program
Abstract: We estimate the effects of high-speed internet in early childhood development exploiting cross-cohort and geographic differences in the introduction of fiber-optic-to-the-home. Using variation in lifetime cumulative exposure to fiber optic and combining survey and administrative data, we estimate effects on cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes measured by validated screening tests. We show that an increase in 10 percentage points in lifetime exposure to fiber optic decreases development scores between 6% and 17% of a standard deviation in communication, problem solving and social skills. An analysis of heterogeneous effects shows that the negative impact is larger for children with more educated parents.

Title: The complementary role of information and contraceptive access in teen pregnancy
Authors: Sevin Kaytan, Stwarth Piedra-Bonilla, Tom Zohar
Abstract: We investigate how information frictions affect the efficacy of contraception provision programs. We study a Costa Rican initiative that combined free access to long-acting reversible contraceptives and a tailored information campaign to correct for baseline misinformation. Using administrative data and geographic variation in the initiative, we find a 16% decrease in the teen birth rate. We show information complements access – an extra year of exposure to the information campaign is equivalent to the effect of contraception access alone. Using surveys on sexual behavior, we show the policy changed the information source from personal networks to healthcare professionals, amending misinformation on sexual health.

Title: The lasting effects of early childhood interventions: The National Vaccination Commando Program in Burkina Faso
Authors: Richard Daramola, Md Shahadath Hossain, Harounan Kazianga, Karim Nchare
Abstract: This study evaluates the long-term effects of a nationwide immunization program in Burkina Faso, known as the National Vaccination Commando Program, implemented in late 1984. Focusing on the measles vaccination component of the program and using a difference-in-differences approach, we find significant reductions in child mortality and improvements in educational attainment, including increased primary and secondary school completion. We also find significant positive effects on adult employment and agricultural productivity, yielding a substantial return on this early health investment. These findings underscore the lasting benefits of early childhood health interventions in low-income countries.

Title: Making information actionable: Experimental evidence from Kenyan courts
Authors: Matthieu Chemin, Daniel L. Chen, Vincenzo Di Maro, Paul Kimalu, Momanyi Mokaya, Manuel Ramos-Maqueda
Abstract: We conduct a randomized controlled trial across Kenyan courts to tackle a major source of court delays: adjournments, i.e., postponements of cases to later dates without reaching a resolution. Partnering with the Kenyan Judiciary, we introduce a simple, cost-effective one-page document that outlines the main reasons for adjournments in each court. We test this intervention in two experimental arms: one where the information is shared with judges, and the other where it is shared with both judges and court user committees. Our intervention successfully prevents approximately 20,000 adjournments nationwide, with each adjournment previously delaying cases by an average of 3 months. The acceleration of court proceedings leads to a notable increase in the demand for and utilization of the legal system, increasing the filing of cases as well as citizen trust in the justice system. Our findings demonstrate that tackling the underlying reasons for court delays can substantially enhance both the perceived and actual performance of judicial systems, fostering greater usage and trust in legal institutions.

Title: Social learning in agriculture: A scalable farmer-to-farmer extension approach for dairy farmers
Authors: Luc Behaghel, Jérémie Gignoux, Karen Macours
Abstract: We evaluate a farmer training intervention for smallholder dairy farmers in Uganda, demonstrating that an at-scale version of the “contact farmer” extension model can significantly increase milk production and be cost-effective. In this model, one “farmer trainer” is selected per village and trained to disseminate knowledge to other farmers. Using experimental sub-treatment arms, and a combination of observed and self-reported data, we assess three key components designed to enhance the program's impact: (i) non-monetary incentives for farmer trainers, (ii) support from professional extension agents, and (iii) a curriculum that combines key principles of animal nutrition and technology choice with a broad set of feeding practices. Results show positive impacts along the hypothesized causal chain, from knowledge acquisition by farmer trainers to knowledge of the farmers they train, and increases in their technology adoption, production, and profits.

Title: Evaluating the environmental and economic implications of curbing transboundary pollution: Evidence from China
Authors: Zeyang Zhang, Yuanyi Xu, Dunhu Chang, Dingding Shao, Xin Wang
Abstract: Mitigating transboundary pollution requires internalizing environmental externalities and coordinating inter-jurisdictional interests. This paper examines the environmental and economic consequences of China's watershed ecological compensation (WEC) policy, a government-led property rights allocation scheme that combines Coasean bargaining with state-contingent contracts. By exploiting the progressive roll-out of inter-provincial WEC schemes and employing a difference-in-difference-in-differences design with a novel county-level dataset containing long-term industrial water pollutant information, we find that upstream counties experience significant reductions in pollution emissions but slower economic growth relative to their adjacent downstream counties after policy implementation. Event study estimates further indicate that environmental governance entailing high economic costs is difficult to sustain over time, reflecting a potential misalignment between costs and benefits in environmental protection. These effects can be attributed to pollution-control-oriented policy measures adopted by upstream local governments and the resulting responses of firms and residents. We further show that upstream local governments' prioritization of environmental governance is shaped by both economic and political incentives. Our findings offer insights into institutional design for improving transboundary water quality in countries with decentralized environmental management systems.

Title: Political empowerment and marital practices
Abstract: Despite decades of reform, early marriage and dowry remain pervasive in rural India. I examine whether women's political representation shifts these practices. I develop a model in which households choose daughters' marriage timing and dowry, facing social penalties for non-marriage. Female leaders, by expanding women's economic opportunities, increase the value of daughters and delay marriage. When social penalties are high, delays raise dowry. I test this using exogenous variation from India's 1992 constitutional amendment, which reserved one-third of village council (pradhan) seats for women. Data from a representative rural survey shows that female pradhans delay marriage by 1.22 years and increase dowry by 68%. A 29% rise in female labor force participation partly explains the delay. Dowry increases are concentrated in patriarchal states, where penalties for non-marriage are most severe. The findings highlight both the potential and the limits of political empowerment in transforming marital norms under binding social constraints.

Title: Time-of-day effects on disclosure of intimate partner violence
Abstract: Efforts to measure and advance research on intimate partner violence (IPV) often rely on the analysis of data collected from confidential household surveys. Yet, even in confidential settings, women may underreport IPV. I present evidence that, in Sub-Saharan Africa, women with husbands who consume alcohol are 6.4 percentage points less likely to self-report severe physical and/or sexual IPV during evening surveys than during morning surveys. This finding occurs because the expected marginal costs of IPV reporting increase over the day with husbands’ alcohol consumption. My back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest that, even if only 10% of interviews conducted by nationally representative IPV survey efforts occur during the evening, time-of-day effects exclude over 314,496 women from estimates of the most severe forms of IPV across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Title: The effects of immigration on agricultural development
Authors: David Escamilla-Guerrero, Andrea Papadia, Ariell Zimran
Abstract: We study the effects of immigration during the Age of Mass Migration (1855–1920) on Brazil’s agricultural development in 1920. Instrumenting for a municipality’s immigrant share using the interaction of aggregate immigrant inflows and the expansion of Brazil’s railway network, we find that a greater share of European immigrants in a municipality led to an increase in farm values. The bulk of the effect was the product of more intense cultivation of land. We also find that it is unlikely that immigration slowed Brazil’s structural transformation. Our results imply that immigration into an emerging agricultural economy can contribute substantially to agricultural development.

Title: The power of electricity: Small hydropower and girls’ education
Abstract: This paper studies the effects of rural electrification on girls' schooling and later life-course outcomes in rural China. We draw on the Rural Electrification through Small Hydropower (SHP-RE), which was rolled out across counties in three waves during the 1980s and 1990s. Using county-cohort data and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate the effects of exposure to electrification by age 15. SHP-RE increased girls' upper-secondary enrollment by 5.1 percentage points, with no comparable gains for boys. The effects are concentrated among cohorts exposed during later childhood and early adolescence. Exposure also delayed women's age at first marriage and reduced the probability of marrying before age 20. Mechanism evidence is most consistent with reduced domestic labor burden for girls and greater adoption of labor-saving household technology. Counties electrified earlier also later exhibited higher shares of women with upper-secondary education or above and greater enterprise-registration density. Overall, the results show that rural electrification generated large and persistent gains for girls and women at key human-capital and life-course margins.

Title: The mental health impact for adolescents ageing out of South Africa’s child support grant
Authors: Tsepang Khumalo, Ronelle Burger, Marisa von Fintel
Abstract: While the benefits of cash transfers are well documented, little attention has been given to the negative effects of their cessation, particularly on mental health. We examined this question using South African longitudinal survey data comprising 7899 unique adolescents tracked as they age out of the Child Support Grant , the country’s largest cash transfer. We find that loss of the Child Support Grant leads to a decline in mental health equivalent to 0.42 of a standard deviation in the CES-D score, robust across model specifications and falsification tests. Increased job search activity points to resource mobilisation as a plausible mechanism, consistent with the Conservation of Resources framework. Effects are concentrated among adolescents in urban areas and households with lower and less diversified income. The results point to a neglected aspect of social protection: how and when cash transfers are withdrawn, particularly when this coincides with critical life stages.

Title: Chronic depression, child development and human capital among the forcibly displaced: Evidence from Syrian refugees
Abstract: A lack of longitudinal data has largely prevented the detection of chronic depression among refugees and its intergenerational associations. I link three years of parental depression measures to children's socio-emotional development and school attendance for Syrian refugees in Jordan. First, chronic depression is common, with over a quarter of adults likely depressed in all three survey rounds. Second, the chronicity of likely parental depression is strongly associated with increasing risk of abnormal child socio-emotional development, and both likely depression and abnormal socio-emotional development are associated with lower school attendance. The results point to caregiver behavior and household tensions as a potential mechanism. Chronic depression among a broadly representative sample of refugees appears to be prevalent and related to urgent child development and human capital needs.

Title: Foreign direct investment, global value chains, and labor rights: No race-to-the-bottom?
Abstract: Does globalization weaken worker's rights? Data is inconclusive; what evidence there is suggests a developing country tends to strengthen labor rights when its access to global value chains (GVC's) increases. We present a stylized model of multinational firms choosing host locations for global value chains, in which each host-country government chooses the strength of collective-bargaining rights for its workers. Each government trades the direct benefit of stronger bargaining rights against the effect of chasing multinationals away to rival countries. We find that an increase in globalization in the sense of lower transaction costs has no effect on equilibrium workers’ rights, but lower costs for one country tend to strengthen that country's labor rights, and adding more countries to the global economy tends, in the limit, to weaken them.
